title: The dice
hookLine: the king of dharma keeps his rule and stakes his kingdom, his brothers, his wife
carry: keeping a rule isn't the same as dharma

cards: Just one more hand. One more bet to win back what you lost on the last one. The Pandavas have done well.

They've built a shining city of their own, Indraprastha, with a hall so magical that Duryodhana, visiting, mistakes a floor for a pool and a pool for a floor, and falls in, and people laugh. He goes home burning.
His uncle Shakuni has an idea. Yudhishthira, the eldest Pandava, can't refuse a challenge. And Shakuni is a master of the dice.

teach.h: HE KNOWS IT'S A TRAP. HE GOES.
teach.b: The invitation comes: a friendly game in the great hall at Hastinapura. Yudhishthira knows it's a trap. He says so, and goes anyway, because a king of his kind doesn't refuse a challenge.
Shakuni throws for Duryodhana. In the popular telling his dice are loaded; the text simply says he's a master of deceit at the game. Yudhishthira stakes a jewel and loses.
His treasury. His whole kingdom. Each time, he's sure the next throw will turn it.
Then Shakuni asks: what else do you have?
Yudhishthira stakes his brothers. The twins first, then Arjuna, then Bhima. He loses every one.
He stakes himself, and loses. The hall is silent. There's one stake you haven't played, says Shakuni: your wife.
And Yudhishthira, the man known for never lying, the son of dharma himself, stakes Draupadi. The dice fall.
Vidura, the king's wise half-brother, has begged them all to stop the game, and no one listens. The other elders, the grandfather Bhishma, the teacher Drona, the blind king, let it go on.
Look at who's playing: not a fool, but Dharmaraja, the king of dharma. Never refuse a challenge: that was his rule, and he kept it, all the way down.

teach.h: HE KEPT THE RULE, LOST ITS POINT.
teach.b: Many teachers read the scene this way: Yudhishthira kept the rule and lost what the rule was for. A king's dharma is to protect the people in his care, and he staked them, one by one.
In that reading, dharma is bigger than any one rule: it's what the rules are there to protect. Tomorrow, what happened to Draupadi in that hall.

how: The dice game in the Sabha Parva is retold in homes, classical dance and theater, and readers often point to it as the moment the great war became hard to stop.

o: a friendly game the Pandavas won to build their city
a rigged game that cost a kingdom, one throw at a time
a contest of archery to choose the next king

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: staked everything, one throw at a time
sat in the hall and let it go on

s: Yudhishthira didn't know the game was a trap
he knew, said so, and went anyway, because he wouldn't refuse a challenge.
he staked his brothers and himself before Draupadi
the twins, Arjuna, Bhima, himself, and then his wife.
he was known for his wisdom and for never lying. that's what makes the scene frightening.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. you know the game is a trap. your rule: a king never refuses a challenge. what does dharma ask of you?
o: play. a rule is a rule.
refuse. your duty is to protect your family and your people.
games.why: many teachers would say refuse: a king's dharma is to protect his people. Yudhishthira played to keep his rule, and staked his kingdom, his brothers, himself and Draupadi.

practice: Think of a rule you hold tight: never back down, never ask for help, never be the one to call first. Ask what Yudhishthira forgot to ask: what is this rule for? Who is it meant to protect?
If keeping it is starting to cost those very people, it isn't dharma anymore. If you pray, ask for the sense to tell the difference.

wordCard.voice: The dice. A rigged game, and a wise man who staked everything, one throw at a time.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dyuta, gambling with dice. The whole episode is called the dyuta.

carryVoice: Your line: keeping a rule isn't the same as dharma. He kept his, and lost his family. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (the hall at Indraprastha; Duryodhana's fall; the dice game, the dyuta)
